items.title: South Africa: the laboratory of Satyagraha (1893–1914)
items.body:
Gandhi (b. 2 Oct 1869, Porbandar) went to South Africa in 1893 for the Dada Abdulla case and stayed till 1914, confronting racial discrimination against Indians. His struggle evolved in two phases: a **moderate phase (1894–1906)** of petitions and memorials, and a **passive-resistance/Satyagraha phase (1906–1914)**.

Key campaigns:

| Grievance | Response |
|---|---|
| Compulsory registration certificates (with fingerprints) | Passive Resistance Association; certificates publicly burned |
| Restrictions on Indian migration | Defied by crossing provinces without licences |
| £3 poll tax on ex-indentured labourers; invalidation of non-Christian marriages | Combined mass campaign |
| Transvaal Immigration Act | Gokhale mobilised opinion; compromise reached |

The successful settlement gave Gandhi the confidence to apply Satyagraha in India.
keyPoints: Gandhi born 2 October 1869 at Porbandar, Gujarat; studied law in England.
Went to South Africa in 1893 (Dada Abdulla case); stayed till 1914.
Founded the Natal Indian Congress and started the newspaper 'Indian Opinion'.
Satyagraha first experimented in South Africa, resting on Truth and Non-violence.
Campaigns targeted registration certificates, the £3 poll tax and invalidation of non-Christian marriages.

items.title: The three early Indian Satyagrahas (1917–1918)
items.body:
After returning in 1915 (on Gokhale's advice he first toured India), Gandhi led three local struggles that established his method and leadership.

| Satyagraha | Year | Cause | 'First' tag | Associates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Champaran | 1917 | Forced indigo (Tin-Kathia) in Bihar | First civil-disobedience-type act | Rajendra Prasad, J.B. Kripalani, Mahadev Desai |
| Ahmedabad Mill Strike | 1918 | Withdrawal of plague bonus | Gandhi's first fast-unto-death | Anasuya Sarabhai |
| Kheda | 1918 | Revenue not remitted despite drought | First no-tax campaign | Sardar Patel |

**Tin-Kathia**: peasants were forced to grow indigo on 3 of every 20 kathas per bigha.
keyPoints: Gandhi arrived in India in 1915; Gopal Krishna Gokhale was his political guru.
Champaran (1917): first Indian Satyagraha, against indigo under the Tin-Kathia system.
Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918): Gandhi's first fast-unto-death; Anasuya Sarabhai assisted workers.
Kheda (1918): first no-tax Satyagraha; Sardar Patel emerged as a leader.
These local wins made Gandhi the undisputed leader of the freedom struggle.

items.title: Gandhi's three great mass movements
items.body:
Gandhi led three all-India movements against British rule.

**Non-Cooperation (1920–22)** — India's first mass movement, fusing the Punjab wrong (Jallianwala/Rowlatt), the Khilafat issue and the demand for Swaraj. Programme: boycott of foreign goods, titles, schools and courts; promotion of khadi and national institutions (Jamia Millia, Kashi Vidyapeeth). Withdrawn after the **Chauri Chaura** violence (Feb 1922).

**Civil Disobedience (1930–34)** — launched with the **Dandi Salt March** (12 Mar–6 Apr 1930) breaking the salt law. The **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** paused it and led Gandhi to the **Second Round Table Conference**.

**Quit India (1942)** — the 'Do or Die' call after the Cripps Mission's failure; a largely leaderless mass upsurge as leaders were jailed.
keyPoints: Non-Cooperation (1920–22): first mass movement; combined Punjab, Khilafat and Swaraj; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922).
Rowlatt Act (1919) was condemned as a 'Black Act'; Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 Apr 1919) under Gen. Dyer followed.
Civil Disobedience began with the Dandi Salt March, 1930.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) took Gandhi to the Second Round Table Conference — the only RTC he attended.
Quit India (Aug 1942) was launched with the slogan 'Do or Die'.

items.title: Gandhian thought: Satyagraha, trusteeship and constructive work
items.body:
**Satyagraha** ('holding to truth') rests on Truth (Satya) and Non-violence (Ahimsa). A Satyagrahi is truthful, fearless and ready to suffer, acting from love — never hatred — for the opponent; its methods are non-payment of taxes, peaceful protest and returning honours.

**Means-ends unity** ('Hind Swaraj', 1909): a pure end can be reached only through pure, non-violent means — the end never justifies impure means.

**Trusteeship**: the wealthy should hold surplus wealth in trust for society.

**Constructive programme**: khadi and the charkha, removal of untouchability (the depressed classes called 'Harijans'; All India Harijan League/Harijan Sevak Sangh, 1932), Hindu-Muslim unity and village self-reliance.

The **Poona Pact (1932)** with Ambedkar replaced separate electorates (Communal Award) with reserved seats for the Depressed Classes.
keyPoints: Satyagraha rests on Truth and Ahimsa; the Satyagrahi suffers willingly and never uses violence.
Means-ends unity: pure ends require pure (non-violent) means (Hind Swaraj, 1909).
Trusteeship: the rich hold surplus wealth in trust for society.
Constructive programme: khadi/charkha, anti-untouchability (Harijan upliftment), Hindu-Muslim unity.
Poona Pact (1932): reserved seats replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
items.source: Gandhi, Hind Swaraj (1909); local APPSC GK PDF — Gandhi Movements

items.title: Titles, martyrdom and the Andhra connection
items.body:
Gandhi converted localised struggles into a national movement, earning the titles **'Mahatma'** and **'Father of the Nation'**. He presided over the INC only once, at the **Belgaum session (1924)**. He was assassinated at Birla House, Delhi, on **30 January 1948** by Nathuram Godse; the day is observed as Martyrs' Day.

**Andhra angle**: the region responded strongly to Gandhi's calls. **Tanguturi Prakasam** ('Andhra Kesari'), **Konda Venkatappayya** and **Pattabhi Sitaramayya** led Congress work, while the nationalist poet **Garimella Satyanarayana** stirred people with patriotic songs (banned by the British). Gandhi toured Andhra promoting khadi, and this mobilisation fed the demand for a separate linguistic Andhra state.
keyPoints: Titles: 'Mahatma' and 'Father of the Nation'.
Presided over the INC only once — Belgaum session, 1924.
Assassinated on 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Godse (observed as Martyrs' Day).
Andhra leaders: Tanguturi Prakasam (Andhra Kesari), Konda Venkatappayya, Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
Poet Garimella Satyanarayana energised Andhra's participation in Gandhian movements.

items.title: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Roles & Writings (PYQ set)
items.body:
## Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) — contents

- Government agreed to: **withdraw ordinances** and prosecutions; **release political prisoners** (those not guilty of violence); permit **coastal salt manufacture** for personal use. Congress agreed to **suspend Civil Disobedience** and attend the **Second Round Table Conference**. It did **not** concede an enquiry into police excesses (a common exam trap).

## Gandhi's roles & positions (PYQ facts)

- Was **instrumental in the abolition of indentured labour** emigration (ended 1917).
- At the **1918 Delhi War Conference (Chelmsford)** Gandhi **supported recruitment** of Indians to the British army (so 'did NOT support' is false).
- After breaking the **Salt Law (1930)** the Government declared the **INC illegal**.
- The 'All India Anti-Untouchability League' (1932) was later renamed the **Harijan Sevak Sangh**.

## Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919)

- Directed against the **Rowlatt (Sedition Committee) Act**; Gandhi used the existing **Home Rule League** organisation to spread it — his first all-India political act.

## Writings, newspapers & titles

- Newspapers/journals: **Indian Opinion** (South Africa), **Young India**, **Navajivan**, **Harijan**.
- Books: **Hind Swaraj (1909)**, autobiography **My Experiments with Truth**, and **'Songs from Prison'** (his translation of Indian devotional lyrics).
- Titles: **'Mahatma'** given by **Rabindranath Tagore**; **'Father of the Nation'** popularised by **Subhas Chandra Bose**. Detained at the **Aga Khan Palace, Pune** during Quit India (1942).
keyPoints: Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 Mar 1931): withdraw ordinances, release non-violent prisoners, allow coastal salt; Congress joins 2nd RTC — but NO enquiry into police excesses.
Gandhi was instrumental in ending indentured labour (1917); at the 1918 War Conference he supported army recruitment; after the Salt Law the INC was declared illegal.
Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) opposed the Rowlatt/Sedition Committee Act; Gandhi used the Home Rule League network.
Newspapers: Indian Opinion, Young India, Navajivan, Harijan; books: Hind Swaraj (1909), My Experiments with Truth, 'Songs from Prison'.
'Mahatma' given by Tagore; 'Father of the Nation' by Bose; Quit India detention at Aga Khan Palace, Pune.
items.mnemonic: Gandhi-Irwin gives 3 releases (ordinances, prisoners, salt) but NOT a police-excess enquiry.
items.source: Standard references — Gandhi-Irwin Pact; Gandhi's roles & writings; UPSC PYQs (2020, 2019, 2021, 2015)
